events.name: 2026 Assam floods

The Hindu reported 98 deaths and more than 155,000 still affected as of 8 August 2026; the Wikipedia infobox lists 100+ deaths and more than 700,000 displaced. Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma ordered door-to-door digital damage assessments. Ongoing as of mid-August 2026.

events.name: 2026 Kenya floods

events.what_happened: Flash floods from the March–May 2026 long rains began on the night of 6–7 March when the Nairobi River burst its banks, killing 23 in the capital that night and disrupting flights at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport. The National Police Service updated the nationwide death toll to 112 on 3 April 2026. About 6,953 households were affected and at least 34,765 people displaced by the end of March. The Kenya Meteorological Department had issued a heavy-rain warning on 25 February.

Wikipedia records 10 deaths, 16,000 people evacuated, 488 homes destroyed and 1,230 damaged, and about CA$1.5 billion in damage. Over 8 feet (2.4 m) of water flooded parts of Chicoutimi and La Baie. Post-flood inquiries found the dike-and-dam network protecting Chicoutimi poorly maintained. The surviving petite maison blanche became the symbol of the flood.

events.what_happened: Meltwater from the Alps plus prolonged rain in the Ardennes, northern France and Germany sent the Rhine, Meuse, Waal and IJssel to record winter levels. On 25 January the Meuse peaked at 45.09 m NAP at Itteren and Borgharen and flooded parts of South Limburg. At Lobith the Rhine reached 16.68 m (usual range 7.2–12 m). From 31 January more than 250,000 residents and 1 million animals were evacuated from Gelderland and Limburg — one of the largest peacetime evacuations in Dutch history. The Waal dike at Ochten shifted and was held with sandbags; primary dikes did not breach. The near-disaster launched the Room for the River and Meuse Works programmes.

Sixteen people died (twelve drowned in Brisbane and Ipswich), about 300 were injured, at least 6,700 homes were flooded and about 13,000 properties were affected. Dutch sea defences failed in many places (67 breaches in Zeeland alone). Wikipedia records 2,551 fatalities overall: 1,836 in the Netherlands, 307 on land in England, 19 in eastern Scotland, 28 in Belgium, and more than 230 at sea including the sinking of MV Princess Victoria. Led to the Delta Works and the Thames Barrier.

events.what_happened: The 1950 Red River flood ran from 15 April to 12 June along the Red River in the Dakotas and Manitoba. Winnipeg was inundated on 5 May (Black Friday). The river reached its highest level since 1861 and flooded more than 1,400 km² of the Red River Valley. An estimated 70,000–100,000 residents were evacuated and four of eleven Winnipeg bridges were destroyed. Wikipedia records 3 deaths in Canada and 5 in the United States. Property losses were estimated at $600 million to $1 billion. The disaster led to construction of the Red River Floodway (Duff's Ditch), completed in 1968.

On 30 May 1948 a railroad embankment that served as Vanport's dike gave way, destroying the wartime city of Vanport — then Oregon's second-largest city — in about an hour. Officially 15 people died; some later estimates are higher. About 18,500 residents were displaced. The city was never rebuilt.

Professional Chinese sources put total deaths from drowning, famine and plague at 400,000–500,000. About five million civilians lived on inundated land until the dikes were repaired in 1947. The river was diverted south into the Huai system for nearly nine years.

About 70% of Louisville was underwater and 175,000 people left their homes. The disaster drove a comprehensive reservoir and levee program on the Ohio.

Affected provinces included Hubei, Hunan, Jiangxi, Anhui, Jiangsu and Zhejiang.

On 25 August dikes near Gaoyou Lake failed; in Gaoyou County alone 18,000 people drowned. Fatality estimates vary widely, from Li Wenhai’s 422,420 (media-based) to official figures around 2 million including famine and disease, and some Western claims of 3.7–4 million.

Water entered Paris through sewers, Metro tunnels and saturated soil rather than by overtopping the quays inside the city. The Seine peaked at 8.62 m above normal on 28 January. Thousands were evacuated; residents moved by boat and wooden walkways. No deaths were reported. Damage was estimated at about 400 million francs.

Water spread across an estimated 50,000 square miles (130,000 km²) of the North China Plain. Wikipedia records at least 930,000 deaths; estimates range from about 900,000 to 2 million including famine and disease. About two million people were left homeless. It is among the deadliest floods on record.

events.what_happened: Weeks of rain and mountain snow from November 1861 into January 1862, capped by a warm atmospheric-river storm, produced the largest flood in the recorded history of California, Oregon and Nevada. The Central Valley became an inland sea 250–300 miles long and about 20 miles wide (about 5,000–6,000 square miles). Sacramento was underwater for months; the state government temporarily moved to San Francisco. Wikipedia cites at least 4,000 deaths in California (about 1% of the state population) and about $100 million damage in 1861 USD.

The National Museum of Australia describes it as Australia's deadliest flood. About 80–100 people died, roughly a third of the town's population. The settlement was later rebuilt on higher ground.

Between Tønder and Emden about 9,000 drowned; the Netherlands had about 2,500 victims. Villages behind the sea dikes in Groningen and East Frisia were devastated. A second storm flood followed in late February.

Dikes failed across the region. The island of Strand was broken apart; Nordstrand and Pellworm remain. Death estimates commonly range from 8,000 to 15,000.

events.what_happened: The All Saints' Flood of 1–2 November 1570 is considered the worst North Sea flood disaster before the 20th century. A surge more than four metres above mean high water overran neglected dikes from Calais to Jutland and Norway. Chroniclers reported that 80 percent of the country was under water; the island of Wulpen in Zeeland was permanently lost. Wikipedia states it was confirmed that the floods drowned 20,000 people and that up to 25,000 deaths can be assumed. Between the Ems and Weser about 10,000 people died. A warning had been issued the morning before — the first documented North Sea flood warning.

events.what_happened: A North Sea storm surge on St. Felix's Day (5 November 1530) breached dikes across Zeeland and Flanders. The town of Reimerswaal was destroyed and never rebuilt as a city. The flood is commonly cited with more than 100,000 deaths and is among the deadliest coastal floods on record in the Low Countries.

events.what_happened: On the night of 18–19 November 1421 a North Sea storm surge broke dikes in the Grote Hollandse Waard. Villages were swallowed and the flood created the freshwater tidal wetlands now known as the Biesbosch. Wikipedia records 2,000–10,000 deaths. Most of the area remained flooded for decades; reclaimed remnants include the island of Dordrecht and the Hoeksche Waard.

events.what_happened: The largest recorded river flood in central Europe. After a prolonged dry spell, days of continuous rain following a Genoa low inundated the Rhine, Moselle, Main, Danube, Weser, Elbe, Vltava and tributaries around the feast of St. Mary Magdalene (22 July 1342). Cologne, Mainz, Frankfurt, Würzburg, Regensburg, Passau and Vienna were seriously damaged. Würzburg's Steinerne Brücke was washed away. In the Danube area alone it is believed about 6,000 people perished. Erosion is estimated at more than 13 billion tonnes of soil.

events.what_happened: A North Sea storm tide on St. Lucia's Day (13–14 December 1287, Old Style) overran seawalls and dikes in the Netherlands and northern Germany. Wikipedia records approximately 50,000 to 80,000 deaths. The island of Griend was nearly destroyed. Formerly landlocked Harlingen became a major Frisian seaport. The same storm killed hundreds in England, including 180 at Hickling, Norfolk, and contributed to the decline of Dunwich.
events.status: Historical. West-Friesland's ringdike largely held; the flood helped end the Friso-Hollandic Wars.

The storm tide destroyed the town of Rungholt on the island of Strand, damaged Ravenser Odd and Dunwich, and destroyed 44 villages. Wikipedia records at least 25,000 deaths, with estimates as high as 100,000. The event is also called the Grote Mandrenke (Great Drowning of Men).

In the Netherlands it was the worst natural disaster of the 19th century, with the heaviest losses in Groningen, Friesland and Overijssel.

More than 100,000 houses were destroyed and about 650,000 people in Tianjin and surrounding areas were made homeless. Japanese forces had also breached 182 dikes on the Daqing, Ziya, Hutuo and Fuyang rivers. Epidemics of cholera, typhoid and dysentery followed. Wikipedia does not give a death toll.

events.what_happened: A night-time cloudburst on 25–26 November 1967 dropped more than 120 mm, mostly in five hours, along a 60 km line from Estoril to Alenquer, coinciding with high tide. Flash floods on small Tagus tributaries struck informal riverside housing around Lisbon. The official death toll is 495; unofficial estimates are at least 700. Newspaper compilations list 522 dead among 2,045 people registered as directly affected. It is Portugal's deadliest flood on record.

Low-lying land in Devon, Somerset, Gloucestershire and South Wales was inundated from Laugharne to above Chepstow. Cardiff was the worst-hit town; St Mary's Church foundations were destroyed. Contemporary and later estimates put the death toll at 2,000 or more; about 200 square miles of farmland were destroyed. Sea water reached Glastonbury Tor, 14 miles inland. After a south-westerly gale drove water toward Finland, the wind reversed from the northeast and pushed the piled-up water back onto the Danish–German coast. Peak water was about 3.3 m above sea level. Eckernförde was the worst-hit German town (78 houses destroyed, 138 damaged). Wikipedia records at least 271 deaths on the Baltic coast, 2,850 houses destroyed or badly damaged, and 15,160 people left homeless. On Falster 52 died; on Lolland 28; 32 died on land in Mecklenburg and West Pomerania.

events.name: All Saints' Flood (1170)
events.geo_source: Amsterdam city centroid; event page says the flood marked the beginning of Amsterdam and pushed seawater to the walls of Utrecht
events.river_or_facility: North Sea coastal barriers / Creil Woods
events.what_happened: A storm surge on the night of 1–2 November 1170 flooded large parts of the northern Netherlands. The Annales Egmundenses, the only contemporary chronicle of the Kennemerland inundation, say livestock drowned and people climbed onto the beams of their houses; ships from Diemen rescued stranded people, and seawater reached the walls of Utrecht. The flood created the islands of Wieringen and Texel, swept away the Creil Woods peat forest between Stavoren and Enkhuizen, and opened the freshwater Almere to the North Sea — the start of the Zuiderzee. It rendered Rotta (predecessor of Rotterdam) uninhabitable and, by dropping the Almere level, dried the mouth of the Amstel enough for Amsterdam later to emerge.
events.status: Historical. Landscape-forming North Sea surge; no sourced death count on the event page.
events.cause_summary: All Saints' Day North Sea storm surge that breached peat barriers and opened the Almere to the sea.
events.notes: Deaths unknown: the dedicated English Wikipedia event page gives no figure. A Europe flood list cites 'probably many thousands'; that estimate is unsourced on the event page and is left in this note only.

events.name: First St. Marcellus's flood (1219)
events.geo_source: Groningen, a principal flooded city in the Dutch sector (same pin as Christmas flood of 1717); Dutch Wikipedia names Noord-Nederland and the Zuiderzee area
events.what_happened: On 16 January 1219, the feast of St. Marcellus, a North Sea storm surge flooded large parts of the northern Netherlands and the Zuiderzee region, as the earlier All Saints (1170), St. Nicholas (1196) and 1214 surges had done. Dutch Wikipedia says the water barely fell with the ebb and the next tide then finished off the remaining dikes. Together with four great storm floods in fifty years this helped open two inland seas, the Zuiderzee and the Wadden Sea. Abbot Emo of Wittewierum left the first surviving eyewitness account of a North Sea storm surge.
events.status: Historical. First St. Marcellus flood; the 1362 Grote Mandrenke is already in the archive.
events.cause_summary: St. Marcellus's Day North Sea storm surge; water stayed high through the ebb so the next tide completed the dike breaches.
events.notes: Dutch Wikipedia infobox lists 36,000 dead. German chronicles cited on secondary pages give ~36,000 (Saxon World Chronicle) or 50,000 (Colmar Annals) and call the figures unreliable. Deaths left null; range 36,000–50,000 stays in this note.

events.name: St. Martin's flood (Sint-Maartensvloed 1686)

events.name: 1982–83 Peru El Niño floods
events.region: Northern coastal departments of Piura and Tumbes
events.geo_source: Piura (same Wikipedia coordinates already used for the 2017 Peru coastal El Niño floods); UPI names Piura and Tumbes and files from Chulucanas
events.what_happened: The 1982–83 El Niño reversed the usual cool Humboldt current and dropped unprecedented rain on Peru's northern coastal desert. A 28 June 1983 UPI dispatch from Chulucanas said 13 feet of rain fell in less than six months on Piura and Tumbes after seven years of drought, flooding farmland, dissolving adobe roads and homes, and killing 230 people. Damage already exceeded $700 million and about 300,000 people were homeless; the government said the twin northern floods and southern drought had devastated 30 percent of the nation's settled land. Academic papers describe localized storms above 100 mm/day focused near Chulucanas.
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 300,000 homeless (UPI, 28 June 1983)
events.cause_summary: 1982–83 El Niño rains on the northern Peruvian desert after a multi-year drought.

sources.label: UPI: 230 die in six months of rain (28 June 1983)

events.notes: 230 is the UPI 28 June 1983 Peru flood death figure for Piura and Tumbes. Global El Niño death estimates of 1,300–2,000 (WHOI) are worldwide and are not copied onto this row.
events.rainfall_mm: 13 feet (~4 m) in less than six months on Piura and Tumbes (UPI, 28 June 1983)
events.economic_damage: More than $700 million in Peru as of June 1983 (UPI)

changelog.change: Added from UPI 28 June 1983 archive and Wikipedia: 1982–83 El Niño event.

events.name: 1987 Bangladesh flood
events.region: Western Brahmaputra / Ganges–Brahmaputra confluence / north of Khulna
events.geo_source: Dhaka (Wikipedia coordinates already used for the 1974/1988/1998 Bangladesh floods); Floods in Bangladesh names the western Brahmaputra, the Ganges–Brahmaputra confluence and areas north of Khulna
events.what_happened: Catastrophic monsoon floods through July and August 1987 inundated 57,300–57,491 km² (about 39–40 percent of Bangladesh), a 30–70 year event on the Floods in Bangladesh page. The worst-hit ground was west of the Brahmaputra, below the Ganges–Brahmaputra confluence, and north of Khulna. The same page's historic-flood table lists 1,657 deaths and 57,491 km² flooded. A companion damage table puts crop losses at 1.5 million tons and financial loss at 35,000 million taka. The Geographical Journal paper by Brammer (1990) is the cited background source for the 1987 and 1988 events.
events.cause_summary: July–August monsoon over the Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna basin; 30–70 year flood.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Floods in Bangladesh (1987 section and historic table)
Brammer 1990, The Geographical Journal (cited on that page)

events.notes: 1,657 is the death figure in the Floods in Bangladesh historic table (Okayama University compilation cited there). No dedicated English Wikipedia event article; the named 1987 section plus the table are the source.
events.return_period: Once in 30–70 years (Floods in Bangladesh / Brammer 1990)
events.inundation_area: 57,300–57,491 km² / about 39–40% of the country (Floods in Bangladesh)
events.economic_damage: 35,000 million taka total financial loss (Floods in Bangladesh damage table)

events.name: 1994 Piedmont / Tanaro flood
events.geo_source: Asti (Wikipedia coordinates 44.90000°N, 8.20694°E); Italian Wikipedia event page photographs and text centre on Asti and names Alessandria (14 dead, ~50% of the city flooded)
events.what_happened: On 4–6 November 1994 torrential rain over southern Piedmont and Liguria sent the Po, Tanaro and tributaries (especially the Belbo) over their banks. Italian Wikipedia's dedicated page records 69 dead, 500 injured and 2,226 displaced in Cuneo, Turin, Asti and Alessandria. Two-day rain peaked at 293.8 mm at Levice (CN); 24-hour totals exceeded 200 mm across the Tanaro, Bormida and Belbo basins. The Tanaro flood wave formed above Ormea on 5 November and reached the Po early on the 7th, with 3,400 m³/s at Farigliano, 4,000–4,200 m³/s at Alba, Asti and Alessandria, and nearly 5,000 m³/s at Montecastello. Ceva, Alba and Asti were about one-third flooded; Alessandria almost half, with 14 dead there.
events.status: Historical. First large emergency for Italy's National Civil Protection Service.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 2,226 displaced (it.wikipedia infobox); Protezione Civile page cites about 5,500 evacuated
events.cause_summary: Three-phase November rainstorm over the Tanaro, Belbo, Bormida and upper Po, with 200–300 mm in 24–48 hours.

sources.label: Dipartimento della Protezione Civile: L'alluvione del Piemonte

events.notes: 69 is the Italian Wikipedia infobox. Protezione Civile's memorial page says 68 victims. Using the dedicated event-page figure; 68 stays in this note.
events.peak_discharge: Nearly 5,000 m³/s on the Tanaro at Montecastello; 3,400 m³/s at Farigliano (it.wikipedia)
events.rainfall_mm: Maximum 264.6 mm in 1 day and 293.8 mm in 2 days at Levice (CN) (it.wikipedia / Luino 1999)

events.name: 2001 Bab El Oued floods
events.geo_source: Bab El Oued (Wikipedia coordinates 36.7907°N, 3.0497°E); OCHA names Bab-El-Oued and Oued Koriche as the worst-hit communes
events.river_or_facility: Oued Koriche / Bab El Oued collectors
events.what_happened: From the evening of 9 November 2001, torrential rain and wind hit northern and western Algeria. In Algiers the Oued Koriche produced a flash flood and mudflow through the hillside communes of Bab El Oued and Oued Koriche. OCHA Situation Report No. 7 (26 November 2001) gave the latest provisional official toll as 751 killed, 700 of them in Algiers, with 170 still missing and 10,000 families (40,000–50,000 people) affected. Seven Algiers communes were seriously hit, four partially. French Wikipedia's Bab El Oued page says torrents of mud engulfed housing and the Place du marché Triolet, killing more than 700 in about three hours. USAID later put damage at more than $300 million.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Up to 10,000 families / 40,000–50,000 people (OCHA sitrep 7, 26 Nov 2001)
events.cause_summary: About 200 mm in 24 hours over the steep, densely built Oued Koriche catchment above Bab El Oued.

sources.label: ReliefWeb: Algeria floods OCHA Situation Report No. 7 (26 Nov 2001)

events.notes: 751 is the Algerian authorities' provisional toll in OCHA sitrep 7 (26 November 2001), of which 700 in Algiers. Academic papers later cite 781 dead and 115 missing, or 750 dead and 120 missing. Later unofficial figures stay in this note.
events.return_period: Described as the Oued Koriche hundred-year flood (Persée / PNUD-FEM 2002)
events.rainfall_mm: On the order of 200–214 mm in 24 hours over Algiers (Persée / weather services cited in academic papers)
events.economic_damage: More than $300 million (GOA / USAID OFDA fact sheet FY2002)

events.name: 2006 Dire Dawa flood
events.geo_source: Dire Dawa (Wikipedia coordinates 9.600°N, 41.867°E); OCHA sitreps name the Dechatu River through the city centre
events.what_happened: On the night of 5–6 August 2006 very heavy rain sent the usually dry Dechatu River through the centre of Dire Dawa, spreading up to 200 m from either bank and sweeping homes, trees and concrete fences. A ReliefWeb Horn of Africa overview (citing figures as of 21 August) said the Dire Dawa flood had left at least 254 people dead with 244 still officially missing; OCHA sitrep 1 had first reported about 200 dead and 300 missing. UNICEF/OCHA Focus on Ethiopia (August 2006) gave 256 dead and 244 missing and said the homes of over 9,000 people were destroyed. The same seasonal floods later killed hundreds more on the Omo and elsewhere; those deaths are not copied onto this row.
events.status: Historical. Named Dire Dawa flash flood, distinct from the wider 2006 Ethiopian season (2016 Ethiopian flood is already in the archive).
events.affected_or_evacuated: About 9,000 displaced in Dire Dawa town plus 7,500 around the city (OCHA/UN appeal figures cited on ReliefWeb)
events.cause_summary: Night-time flash flood on the Dechatu after very heavy rain over a deforested catchment with houses built too close to the channel.

sources.label: ReliefWeb: Regional overview of flooding in the Horn of Africa (Dire Dawa 254 dead as of 21 Aug 2006)
ReliefWeb: Ethiopia Dire Dawa Floods — OCHA Situation Report No. 2

events.notes: 254 is the confirmed Dire Dawa toll as of 21 August 2006 on the ReliefWeb Horn overview. Focus on Ethiopia (Aug 2006) cites 256 dead. Wider 2006 Ethiopia season deaths (639 nationwide as of 27 August in that overview) are not used here.

events.name: 2007 South Asian floods
events.geo_source: Patna city centroid; Bihar and Uttar Pradesh were the hardest-hit Indian states on the dedicated event page (same pin style as flood-south-asia-2017)
events.what_happened: From 3 July to 15 August 2007 monsoon floods struck India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan and Pakistan. Wikipedia's dedicated event page, citing Indian and Bangladeshi governments, puts the death toll in excess of 2,000, with about 20 million affected by 3 August and 30 million in India, Bangladesh and Nepal by 10 August. A USAID/OFDA regional fact sheet compiled later official tallies: India 2,253 dead and 43 million affected (Government of India, 28 August); Bangladesh 563 dead and 10.7 million affected (IFRC, 4 September); Nepal 146 dead (OCHA, 21 August); Pakistan 420 dead (OCHA, 27 August). In Bangladesh the Padma and Brahmaputra flooded; the Dhaka highway was cut; by 15 August about five million people were still displaced.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 43 million affected in India (GOI 28 Aug 2007); ~30 million in India, Bangladesh and Nepal by 10 August (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Exceptionally heavy South Asian monsoon from early July 2007 on the Ganges–Brahmaputra system.

sources.label: ReliefWeb: South Asia Regional Floods Fact Sheet #2 FY2007 (USAID/OFDA)

events.notes: 2,253 is the Government of India figure as of 28 August 2007 (USAID/ReliefWeb Fact Sheet #2). Wikipedia infobox says 2,000+ regional. Bangladesh, Nepal and Pakistan sitrep totals are not added onto this India-pinned row.
events.economic_damage: More than $2 billion in India (GOI / USAID fact sheet); Bangladesh agriculture about $294 million (DAE / IFRC)

events.name: 2009 European floods
events.region: Czech Republic / Austria / Poland / Slovakia / Hungary / Romania
events.geo_source: Nový Jičín city centroid; the event page describes 24 June flash floods on the Jičínka (5.5 m, 2 m above the 1997 flood) with multiple deaths in that district
events.what_happened: June 2009 rain from a slow-moving upper low flooded the Oder, Vistula, Elbe and Danube basins in the Czech Republic, Austria, Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, Germany, Romania, Serbia and Turkey. Wikipedia's infobox lists 33 fatalities. In the Czech Republic persistent rain from 22 June and a 24 June two-hour flash flood (up to 80 L/m²) on the Jičínka and Zrzávka killed people in Nový Jičín district; the page later says fourteen people died in the Czech Republic. Austria had its wettest June on record in the north (Lunz am See 207 mm/48 h; St. Pölten 311 mm in June). Turkey's 9 September Istanbul flash flood, treated as a further storm on the same page, killed 20.
events.status: Historical. Named Central European June 2009 floods; a Czech complement to 1997/2002/2013 already on file.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Thousands of firefighters deployed in Austria; 50 families evacuated in Kraków (Wikipedia)
events.cause_summary: Quasi-stationary June upper low (Quinton) over the Alps, Balkans and Black Sea, then local thunderstorms on saturated ground.
events.notes: 33 is the English Wikipedia infobox total for the dedicated 2009 European floods page. The lead cites at least 12 dead in the Czech Republic and one in Poland; the Czech section later says 14. The same page's 'Further storms' section includes the 9 September 2009 Istanbul flash flood (20 dead), which is not the June Central Europe wave. Using the page infobox; composition stays in this note.
events.rainfall_mm: Lunz am See 207 mm in 48 h; Nový Jičín area up to 80 L/m² in two hours on 24 June (Wikipedia)
events.economic_damage: First Czech estimates 5–6 billion Kč (~€230 million); Lower Austria claims about €60 million (Wikipedia)

events.name: 2025 Yemen floods
events.geo_source: Sana'a city centroid; ReliefWeb disaster page covers a nationwide season across 19–20 governorates
events.what_happened: Yemen's second rainy season produced widespread flash floods from 1 August 2025. OCHA's mid-September sitrep recorded about 50,600 households (around 354,400 people) affected in 125 districts in 19 governorates, with 62 deaths and 95 injuries, mainly from drowning, lightning and falling debris. ECHO's 30 September Daily Flash, citing UN OCHA as of 29 September, raised the tally to 82 dead, 100 injured and nearly 455,500 people affected across 156 districts in 20 governorates. IDP sites were among the worst hit. April–July 2025 rains (20 deaths) were a separate earlier spell.
events.status: Season closed; recovery ongoing in a pre-existing humanitarian crisis.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Nearly 455,500 people across 156 districts in 20 governorates as of 29 September 2025 (UN OCHA via ECHO Daily Flash 30 September)
events.cause_summary: Second-season (July–September) rains and flash floods across Yemen, hitting IDP sites especially hard.

sources.label: ReliefWeb: Yemen Key Message Update, September 2025 (FEWS NET)
ReliefWeb: ECHO Daily Flash 30 September 2025 (OCHA 82 dead)

events.notes: 82 deaths and 100 injured are the 29 September 2025 UN OCHA figures as cited by ECHO on 30 September. The 17 September OCHA/FEWS NET sitrep had 62 dead and 95 injured; that earlier dated figure stays in this note.

events.name: 2026 Yemen floods
events.region: Taiz (Al-Mokha) and more than ten governorates
events.geo_source: Taiz city centroid; IFRC/ECHO name Al-Mokha, Mawza and Al-Wazeyah districts of Taiz as the worst-hit coastal ground
events.what_happened: Yemen's 2026 rains began early (from 20 March) and intensified from 27 March, flooding more than ten governorates including Taiz (Al-Mokha), Al Jawf, Ibb, Abyan, Al Bayda, Lahj, Marib, Al Hodeidah, Hadramout, Aden and Al Dhale'e. The IFRC DREF (MDRYE017, 6 April 2026) cited Yemen Red Crescent Society figures of 83,713 people (11,959 households) affected, at least 30 dead and 47 injured, and 254 incidents logged at the YRCS emergency centre. ECHO's 31 March flash said at least 15 dead and 9,820 households affected on the west coast, including 49 IDP sites. A later ECHO note (30 April) gave at least 24 dead and 7,900 households along the west coast.
events.status: Ongoing seasonal flooding as of April 2026 sitreps.
events.affected_or_evacuated: 83,713 people / 11,959 households (YRCS / IFRC DREF 6 April 2026)
events.cause_summary: Early, intense first rainy season from 27 March 2026, worst on the Taiz–Hodeidah west coast and in IDP sites.

events.name: 2025 Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei floods
events.geo_source: Miyun District (Wikipedia coordinates 40.37444°N, 116.83944°E); Chinese Wikipedia and Reuters name Miyun (Taishitun nursing home) as the deadliest site
events.river_or_facility: Miyun Reservoir / Panjiakou Reservoir / Qingshui River
events.what_happened: From 23–29 July 2025 a stalled trough, with indirect influence from Typhoon Co-May (Zhujiecao), produced extreme rain over Beijing, northern Hebei and northern Tianjin. Chinese Wikipedia records at least 64 dead and 39 missing: 44 dead in Beijing (all at a Taishitun, Miyun, elderly-care centre), 16 dead in Luanping County, Hebei, and 4 dead in Tianjin, mainly in Jizhou mountain floods. Reuters on 31 July reported at least 60 dead, including 31 at the Miyun care home, and 573.5 mm in parts of Miyun — about a year's rain in a few days. Hebei reported 356,000 people affected and 44,000 relocated by 29 July. A June 2026 emergency-management investigation blamed the care-home deaths on a Qingshui River extreme flood inundating a low-lying site.
events.affected_or_evacuated: Hebei 356,000 affected and 44,000 relocated as of 29 July; Beijing more than 80,000 evacuated (zh.wikipedia / Xinhua cited there)
events.cause_summary: Week-long July rainstorm over the Yanshan hills, indirectly steered by Typhoon Co-May, with a Qingshui River flash flood through Miyun.

sources.label: Reuters: Care home residents among at least 60 killed in north China flooding (31 July 2025)

events.inundation_area: Hebei crops 72,000 ha affected as of 29 July (zh.wikipedia)
events.economic_damage: Direct losses in the north described as exceeding 100 billion yuan on the Chinese Wikipedia page

events.name: Cyclone Ditwah floods
events.region: Sri Lanka (worst in Kandy, Nuwara Eliya, Badulla) / Tamil Nadu
events.geo_source: Kandy (Wikipedia coordinates 7.2931°N, 80.635°E); Cyclone Ditwah page lists 234 of 644 Sri Lankan deaths in Kandy District
events.what_happened: Cyclonic Storm Ditwah crossed Sri Lanka from 26 November 2025 and then paralleled the Tamil Nadu coast. Wikipedia's dedicated storm page records 647 fatalities (644 in Sri Lanka, 3 in India), 21 injured, 183 missing and more than $4.14 billion damage. Sri Lanka had 234 deaths in Kandy District, 90 in Badulla, 89 in Nuwara Eliya and further deaths across 18 districts; 6,200 homes were destroyed and 96,545 damaged; about 1.46 million people (407,594 families) were affected and 59,000 families sheltered in 1,529 centres. The Mavil Aru bund breached in Trincomalee District. It was Sri Lanka's deadliest disaster since the 2004 tsunami. A DMC sitrep of 16 December 2025 is cited for the district table.
events.status: Recovery ongoing into 2026 (bailey bridges still being installed under Operation Sagar Bandhu).
events.affected_or_evacuated: 1.46 million people / 407,594 families affected; 59,000 families in 1,529 centres (Wikipedia / DMC)
events.cause_summary: Slow-moving cyclonic storm that stalled over Sri Lanka and dumped extreme rain on central-highland catchments.
events.notes: 647 is the Wikipedia infobox (644 Sri Lanka + 3 India). A DMC sitrep of 16 December 2025 is the cited source for the Sri Lankan district table. Not a dam failure; the Mavil Aru bund breach is noted as a tank overflow, not copied as a structural dam-collapse toll.
events.economic_damage: World Bank about Rs 1.3 trillion / US$4.1 billion; government Rs 1.03 trillion / US$3.4 billion (Wikipedia)
